name: Egyptian nationalism
summary: Egyptian nationalism is a mostly civic, territorial nationalism that defines the nation by Egypt, its Nile Valley land and its cultural heritage, uniting Muslims and Copts. In its liberal-era form it demanded an end to British occupation, a constitution and elected parliament under a constitutional monarchy, Egyptian ownership of the economy, and the unity of Egypt and Sudan. It stressed Egypt's distinctness from the wider Arab and Islamic worlds.
scope: The liberal territorial strand from Urabi and Mustafa Kamil through the 1919 revolution, the Wafd of Saad Zaghloul, Ahmed Lutfi al-Sayyid, Pharaonism of Taha Hussein, Talaat Harb's economic nationalism and the 1923 constitution, to 1952. Excludes Nasser's pan-Arabism and Islamist critics such as Hassan al-Banna, which have separate profiles. The movement had little to say on many modern social and economic issues, so many answers are low-confidence inferences or 0.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Wafd-era nationalists built schools and conciliation boards but left no healthcare doctrine; a state duty to citizens' welfare is inferred from the liberal-national programme of raising the nation's standards.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Wafd set up labor conciliation boards yet enacted no significant labor laws, and nationalists took no stated line on wage floors, so adherents are split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Economic nationalism backed private Egyptian enterprise (Bank Misr) but wanted national ownership over open foreign-dominated markets; no doctrine on markets versus government.

public-ownership.rationale: Interwar economic nationalism sought Egyptian private shareholders owning banks and industry rather than state ownership; nationalisation came only with the later Nasser regime.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Wafd was a centre-right liberal-conservative party led by landowners, and sources record no stated taxation programme.

unions-good.rationale: The Wafd tried labor councils but would not change the government's anti-union policy; its attitude to unions was supportive in rhetoric and limited in practice.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1923 constitution declares property inviolable, allowing expropriation only for public interest with fair compensation.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Talaat Harb criticised foreign firms and idle foreign capital serving non-Egyptian ends, implying support for curbing foreign-controlled corporations; general corporate regulation is inferred.

cut-welfare.rationale: No welfare programme to cut existed in the nationalist platform; the sources give no position.

worker-ownership.rationale: Economic nationalism favoured Egyptian shareholder-owned firms, not worker ownership; inferred from the Bank Misr model.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The constitution protects privacy of letters and telegraphs but allows limits by law and martial law; modern counter-terror surveillance was never addressed.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Public morals limit freedoms in the 1923 constitution and the movement was socially conservative; drugs are inferred as unwelcome.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The constitution guarantees free opinion within the law and stresses Muslim-Christian unity, but no stated stance on hate speech law exists.

strong-leader.rationale: Wafd politics centred on the charismatic Zaghloul yet the slogan put the nation above the government and championed parliament; adherents split.

state-harmful.rationale: The movement demanded a sovereign constitutional Egyptian state; the 1923 constitution establishes one with sovereignty vested in the nation.

limit-guns.rationale: No stated position; gun control was not an issue in the liberal-era nationalist programme.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nationalists opposed British-controlled forces but wanted an Egyptian army under parliament; funding questions were not defined.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The constitution safeguards public order and morals and the nationalists were socially conservative; inferred disagreement.

decide-locally.rationale: The 1923 constitution creates provincial and municipal councils but builds a unified, indivisible state; centralised national unity was the aim.

rehabilitation.rationale: The constitution enshrines legality of crime and punishment but no penal philosophy is stated.

traditional-family.rationale: Liberal-era nationalism modernised education but remained socially conservative and Islamic-Christian in culture; support for traditional family is inferred.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not an issue in the movement; adherents' culture and the constitution's public morals clause imply firm disagreement.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from socially conservative Egyptian norms and the morals clause.

more-religion-public.rationale: Nationalists united Muslims and Copts under crescent and cross and made Islam the state religion without a theocracy, so adherents are split on greater public role.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Race was not an organising theme except for Egypt's attitude to Sudan; no stated position.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not discussed; inferred from socially conservative norms despite support for girls' schooling.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Egyptian nationalism is defined by Egyptian culture and heritage, from Pharaonism to the 1923 preamble's insistence on keeping national qualities of historic heritage.

gradual-change.rationale: The movement combined mass revolution in 1919 with negotiation and constitutional gradualism, so no single line prevails.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The constitution reserves public posts for Egyptians but immigration levels were not an issue in the era.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Nationalists appealed to the Paris Peace Conference and Wilsonian self-determination, but resisted foreign supervision of Egypt; giving international bodies more power is inferred as unwelcome.

free-trade.rationale: Economic nationalism aimed at Egyptian-owned industry and finance against foreign dominance, which implies scepticism of unrestricted free trade.

nation-first.rationale: Egyptian nationalism puts Egypt's independence and interests first against both British dominance and wider Arab or Islamic projects.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: A movement fighting foreign occupation was wary of foreign intervention; inferred.

open-borders.rationale: Territorial nationalism with Egyptian-only public posts; open borders is inferred as opposed.

limit-growth.rationale: Nationalists wanted industrial growth through Bank Misr's companies; inferred disagreement.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Tahtawi and the Nahda embraced European learning and modern schooling as the route to national advancement; inferred optimism.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic for the liberal-era movement; no position.

revolution-justified.rationale: The 1919 revolution was the movement's peak and Urabi's rising predated it, so popular uprising against occupation is accepted.

experts-over-public.rationale: No stated position; the Wafd stressed popular sovereignty yet its leaders were elite professionals.

central-planning.rationale: Nationalist economics favoured private Egyptian capital over planning; planning arrived under Nasser.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed by the liberal-era movement.

land-value-tax.rationale: No stated position; the Wafd's landowning base suggests no support, but it is uncertain.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The Wafd was liberal-conservative with landowning leaders; inferred disagreement.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Harb's Banque Misr aimed at building Egyptian-owned industry, textiles and others, a programme of national economic protection.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Banque Misr directed investment through a private national bank rather than the state; the state-led approach came later under Nasser.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Nationalists explain history through national identity and foreign domination, not production relations; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: The liberal-era sources record no competition-policy stance, and Banque Misr built large combined Egyptian firms, so the movement is split.

no-bailouts.rationale: No source records a view on rescuing failed firms; a neutral answer reflects that the movement's economics were about ownership, not bailouts.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The 1923 constitution sets a rule-of-law framework with legality of crimes and a Privy Council; inferred that constraints on majorities are accepted.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The 1923 constitution gave suffrage to men only in practice and no quotas existed; inferred disagreement.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Egypt sought a nationally owned economy but not a closed bloc with colonies; Egypt held none to bloc with.

moral-incentives.rationale: Capitalist national-bank approach relied on material incentives; inferred.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The 1919 revolution was a mass movement of strikes, petitions and demonstrations led by a delegation, not a vanguard armed group.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The 1923 constitution established a hereditary monarchy and let the King grant titles, though it also says Egyptians are equal before the law.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Pharaonism built national identity on an unbroken ancient Egyptian history, and the 1923 preamble cites the ancient historical greatness of the people.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The movement demanded an end to the protectorate and British tutelage; it rejected Cromer-style claims that Egyptians needed foreign rule.

patriotic-education.rationale: Mustafa Kamil stressed education, order and love of homeland and founded a national school; patriotism taught in schools is consistent.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not an Egyptian issue; no position.

public-money-creation.rationale: Harb wanted a national bank; whether money creation should be public was not argued.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Not addressed by the liberal-era movement.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid opposed pan-Ottoman and pan-Islamic ties, and nationalists stressed Egyptian-only interests; neo-imperial influence is inferred as unwelcome.

delink-world-market.rationale: Nationalists wanted Egyptian ownership within the world economy, not withdrawal from it.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Marxist concept foreign to the movement.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Article 3 of the 1923 constitution bars discrimination on origin, language or religion in rights and public duties.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The 1923 constitution included a bill of rights in Part II and was a core Wafd achievement.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The nationalists rejected the protectorate and British-imposed terms, including Milner's proposals, as having no legitimate force.

elective-rulers.rationale: The movement accepted a hereditary constitutional monarchy under Article 1, though relations with the Palace were cool.

minority-veto.rationale: The 1923 system ran on majority parliamentary rule; individual vetoes were not part of it.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Wafd slogan held the nation above the government, and the movement resisted king and Britain when they overrode the constitution.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal welfare was not an issue in the nationalist programme, and no source gives a position, so it is left neutral.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The sources never discuss animal use; adherents had no stated doctrine either way.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wafd leadership was landowning but no doctrine of duty was stated.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement was a mass participatory political struggle in 1919, with strikes and petitions in every town.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Nationalists used press and popular culture, such as Sanu's satire, to mobilise; the thesis is a critical-theory idea.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Nationalists criticised foreign capital and occupation burdens, but no world-systems theory was stated.

native-born-offices.rationale: Article 3 reserves public positions, civil or military, to Egyptians save in exceptional conditions.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Harb's national bank was meant to fund development from Egyptian savings rather than foreign capital.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Nationalists claimed Sudan as Egyptian territory and demanded its unity with Egypt; the principle of recovering lost territory is inferred from that.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: The movement predates the post-war antifascist constitutions and its sources never discuss fascism; the Blue Shirts even imitated European uniformed movements.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The liberal nationalists did not address fascism and communism as a pair, so no position can be sourced.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: This is an American historical controversy that Egyptian nationalist sources never touch.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Not addressed; nationalists did make ancient monuments, like Tutankhamun's tomb, a national symbol.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gender-disadvantage programmes of this kind did not exist in the era, and no source states a view.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources contain nothing on domestic violence policy, so neither side can be attributed.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Liberal-era nationalists wanted advanced Western-style constitutional institutions; the preamble says so, though also with national distinction.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The 1923 constitution subordinates the army to law and parliament; the military rose to politics after 1952.

paid-care-work.rationale: Wages for household labour was not an issue for the liberal-era movement, whose sources are silent on it.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from Egyptian cultural conservatism; no source states it.

office-by-exam.rationale: The constitution provides equal access to public posts; merit hiring is inferred.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Harb's project aimed at keeping key banking, shipping and industry in Egyptian hands against foreign control.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from socially conservative norms.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Article on parliament says members represent the whole nation, and voters may not bind them.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design was not on the nationalist agenda, and the sources give no indication of preference.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Property is inviolable in the 1923 constitution; community land tenure conflicts with it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1923 constitution requires the budget to be presented to Parliament for examination and approval before the financial year.

single-official-language.rationale: Article on the state says Arabic is its official language, but another article leaves private and public-meeting use of any language unrestricted.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Economic nationalists resented foreign holdings but no ban is stated.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The 1923 constitution bars discrimination by origin, language or religion in law, but disparate-impact doctrine is a later concept not discussed.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Mass consumerism was not a concern in the era, and the sources record no view.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The movement itself was a victim of foreign intervention; no support for arming insurgents is documented.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Nationalists rejected foreign troops dictating Egypt's course and the protectorate; inferred.

corporate-influence.rationale: Harb's criticism of foreign capital suggests distrust of corporate influence, though not stated about lobbying.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Economic nationalism resisted foreign control of the national economy; inferred for NGOs and media.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Population policy is not discussed in the nationalist sources, so adherents have no stated position.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local residence limits on property purchase were not debated; the economic nationalists focused on national, not local, ownership.

job-guarantee.rationale: No source credits the Wafd-era movement with a state employment guarantee; labor policy there was limited to conciliation boards.

democratic-peace.rationale: This political-science thesis is anachronistic for the movement, whose sources never discuss it.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Constitutional nationalists affirmed law-bound government though they disobeyed colonial authority; inferred.

non-intervention.rationale: Opposition to British interference in Egypt's affairs was central to the movement's identity.

industrial-unions.rationale: The Wafd only experimented with local conciliation boards and a labor council, and nothing states a preferred union structure.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The movement stressed Muslim-Christian unity and Mustafa Kamil's motto was Free in our country, hospitable to all.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Not a position of this movement; inferred.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The constitution protects press freedom but no access-to-information right.

local-production.rationale: Economic nationalism favoured domestic production but not necessarily locally.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty clauses place Egyptian law and sovereignty first, though the treaty article lets the King conclude treaties with parliamentary approval where needed.

religious-nation.rationale: The liberal nationalists defined Egypt territorially across Muslims and Copts, symbolised by the crescent and cross of 1919, and Lutfi al-Sayyid rejected religion as the basis of nationhood.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The movement rejected British dominance and the protectorate, refusing subordination.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The constitution sets a unified state budget; regional fiscal autonomy is not part of the programme.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The question presumes a communist distinction between personal and productive property; the movement protected all property and never drew that line.

defeat-communism.rationale: Not a doctrine of the liberal-era movement.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The liberal-era sources contain no view on mixed public service delivery, so it is left neutral.

religion-illusion.rationale: Islam is the state religion and freedom of belief is protected; the nationalists were not atheist.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The movement's economic nationalists built capitalist firms but never wrote about capitalism's historical role, so no position is sourced.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Women's equality arguments in the period centred on schooling and the vote, not economic transformation, and no source states this view.

socialized-care.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from socially conservative norms.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Hussein and Sanu used Egyptian Arabic and modernised vocabulary; purism was not part of Egyptian nationalism.

treaties-binding.rationale: The movement rejected imposed treaties like the protectorate, but the question concerns indigenous-state treaties, which have no Egyptian analogue.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Nationalist economics favoured a national bank and industry, not small cooperative communes.

majority-settlement.rationale: Constitutional equality of all Egyptians contradicts policies of settlement against minorities.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Nationalists were mostly liberal; the idea of a third way is more Nasserist.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Pharaonism grounds Egypt's identity in the same land since 3100 BC; the broader claim is inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: No position; inferred as not part of the movement.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the public morals clauses and social conservatism.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Wafd politics sought a representative parliament and condemned palace and British suppression; the 1923 constitution guarantees association.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Freedom of belief is absolute under the constitution, but Islam is the state religion; split.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The movement fought for ending a colonial protectorate in which Egypt's economy was harnessed to the British war effort.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Kamil's nationalism had Islamic and Ottoman links but liberal territorial nationalism did not use jihad doctrine.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid rejected religion as the basis of authority, and Wafd politics ran through parliament.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The Wafd was a mass party but a representative one.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectional analysis is a late-twentieth-century idea absent from these sources.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from social conservatism.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The Wafd claimed to represent the whole nation across classes, but the sources do not discuss left and right as categories.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist alienation theory was not part of the liberal nationalist programme.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The nationalists were themselves overwhelmingly Muslim and Christian Egyptians, and held that Islam was Egypt's state religion.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The 1923 constitution states that all powers emanate from the nation, and the Wafd's claim rested on popular sovereignty.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Freedom of religious rites is safeguarded; no position on dress.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Workplace nondisclosure law is a modern issue that the movement could not have addressed.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Wafd was liberal-conservative; no stated economic model.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The constitution provides for an army, conscription and martial law; the movement demanded an Egyptian army under national control.

rich-first.rationale: Egyptian economic nationalists wanted national development but the sources do not discuss uneven growth by region or group.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Not addressed for Cold War blocs; the later Nasser era is another strand.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The constitution makes the monarchy hereditary under Article 1, with the Wafd accepting it as a constitutional monarchy.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Harb's bank was a conventional interest-earning shareholder bank.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The constitution protects debt obligations in the budget, and Egyptian debt issues were tied to foreign control, so adherents' stance on lender conditions is unsourced.

property-franchise.rationale: The constitution says Egyptians are equal in political rights; a property franchise is not part of the nationalist demands.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminist theory is outside the movement's frame of reference.

reification.rationale: This is a Marxist critical-theory concept that does not appear in the nationalist sources.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The constitution protects press freedom without comment on ownership.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Articles 5 and 6 of the 1923 constitution require arrest and punishment only under law, no punishment for acts before the law.

racial-franchise.rationale: Article 3 bars discrimination in civil and political rights on grounds of origin, language or religion.

online-participation.rationale: Internet participation is anachronistic for a movement of the 1880s to 1950s.

open-government-data.rationale: Open data is a modern concept; the movement's sources are silent on it.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The movement stressed Muslim-Christian unity but family law was left to religious communities; low confidence.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The movement's unity of crescent and cross contradicts sectarian boycotts.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Randomly selected assemblies are a modern device that this movement never considered.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Nationalists generally favoured modernisation; Lutfi al-Sayyid argued utility over religious identity, but no stated doctrine on reform.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The landowning Wafd leadership did not argue that wealth concentration threatens freedom, though economic nationalists disliked foreign control.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Not an issue for the movement; its sources contain no relevant position.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Islam is the state religion and freedom of belief is absolute.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The constitution presupposes police, arrests under law and punishments.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The movement achieved Muslim-Copt unity without power-sharing quotas.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: No source gives the nationalists a view on charity versus state welfare, so adherents are treated as split.

term-limits.rationale: Term limits were not part of the constitutional design for a hereditary king and an elected House, and the movement's sources never raise them.

vote-delegation.rationale: Constitutional parliament with members representing the nation; delegation not envisaged.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk is a modern concern that this movement could not have addressed.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The sources do not describe marriage authority doctrine; the movement favoured girls' schooling but left family law to religious communities.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Article 3 reserves political rights for Egyptians.

rent-control.rationale: Housing rents were not a nationalist programme item and the sources give no position.

abolish-ip.rationale: Intellectual property abolition was not discussed; Banque Misr-style industrial firms had no stated stance either.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The Wafd's Blue Shirts used a uniformed youth wing with the motto Obedience and Struggle, and Young Egypt used green shirts, but other strands did not; split.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear weapons did not exist for most of the movement's life, so no position is attributable.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Nationalists demanded evacuation of British troops; foreign bases were the core grievance.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Formal recognition of past genocides is a modern politics the liberal-era sources do not discuss.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The movement defended property and ownership returns, and the sources record no argument on labour versus capital income.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Not a position of this movement.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Pharaonism explicitly claimed an unbroken Egyptian national identity from ancient times to the modern era.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Constructionist theory about sex is a late-twentieth-century academic position absent from these sources.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: This is a post-structuralist feminist thesis foreign to the movement.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The 1919 revolution's dead became national martyrs and the movement honoured them.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Territorial nationalism rested on utility and history, not spiritual struggle.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Egyptian nationalism concerns a homeland population in Egypt itself, not a diaspora gathering, so the question does not map onto it.

culture-before-state.rationale: The movement put independence and a constitution first, with cultural renewal alongside.

god-not-male.rationale: Theology of divine gender is not part of the nationalist sources.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Feminist scriptural criticism is not part of the sources on this movement.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Banque Misr stressed Egyptian ownership and staffing against foreign-dominated finance; the majority-versus-minority framing is inferred.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Egyptian nationalists sought unity of Egypt and Sudan but never discussed merging administrative regions for one people.

independent-unions.rationale: Not addressed apart from the Wafd's unwillingness to confront anti-union policy.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Socialist definitions were not the movement's concern and the sources contain nothing on this.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The sources record no view on public ownership of water or hospitals; national banking and industry dominate the economic record.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1923 constitution created a Senate alongside the House of Representatives.

municipal-property.rationale: Property is inviolable under the constitution; municipal ownership of production is not nationalist doctrine.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The constitution makes Egypt a single indivisible sovereign state.

family-wage.rationale: The sources on the Wafd and Banque Misr do not mention family wage doctrine.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Drug regulation is a modern issue the movement never addressed.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Ageing research funding is anachronistic and absent from the sources.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Digital anonymous payments are a modern topic with no counterpart in the movement's sources.

online-anonymity.rationale: Online anonymity is anachronistic for this movement.

person-over-state.rationale: The constitution protects individual liberties, but the movement's ideal subordinated individuals to national independence.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Religion is part of national life under the constitution; inferred.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Provincial and municipal councils under the 1923 constitution are created and regulated by national law.

gm-crops.rationale: Genetically modified crops are a modern question the nationalist sources cannot answer.

dense-cities.rationale: Urban density and environment were not a concern of the liberal-era movement.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The movement was civic and unity-minded across religions; racial organisation is not part of it.

racial-pride.rationale: Pharaonism emphasises pride in ancestry as national heritage, but not race itself as an organising principle.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The constitution lets the King declare war only with parliamentary consent; no stated doctrine.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid insisted Egyptians are not Arabs and Taha Hussein rejected pan-Arabism, so language does not define the nation.

communal-electorates.rationale: The movement stressed one national community without sectarian division, and the Copts resisted separate electorates.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The movement saw Britain as working against Egyptian unity with Sudan, but a general partition plot is inferred.

free-public-college.rationale: The constitution makes only primary education free and compulsory.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Nationalists defended property and Egyptian ownership but sources give no stance on its distribution among small owners.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Harb's Banque Misr was a money-based, wage-employing national enterprise; abolition is alien to the movement.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The movement wanted a national bank under Egyptian control; abolishing central banks is not in its programme.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Wafd set up local labor conciliation boards and sought a national labor council, but not state-recognised wage and price setting.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Wafd fought for a multi-party parliament, won 179 of 211 seats in 1924 in contested elections, and was banned only when Nasser dissolved parties in 1953.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Article 1 of the 1923 constitution set up a representative hereditary monarchy, which the Wafd accepted in its constitutional form.

democracy-best.rationale: The Wafd's slogan put the nation above the government and it championed an elected parliament, though its commitment was tested by elite politics.

direct-votes.rationale: The 1923 constitution is representative, with deputies representing the whole nation; direct legislation was not proposed.

workers-councils.rationale: The movement's constitutional goal was a parliament, with workers' councils absent from its programme.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nationalists demanded the unity of Egypt and Sudan and the constitution calls the monarchy indivisible; Sudan's separation was resisted.

natural-rulers.rationale: Wafd leaders were a landowning and professional elite, but its ideology was popular sovereignty; no stated view.

political-violence-never.rationale: The 1919 revolution included strikes and some rural attacks on British installations, and Egyptians formed secret armed groups; violence was not renounced.

war-builds-character.rationale: Mustafa Kamil criticised Muhammad Ali's militarist state; glorifying war is not a stated doctrine.

separate-church-state.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid rejected religion as the basis of nationhood and freedom of belief is absolute, but Islam was made the state religion.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The 1923 constitution makes Islam the state religion yet bases law on parliament and the nation as the source of power; Sharia was added by Sadat later.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The constitution gives the state an army, courts and a Privy Council; privatising them is alien to the movement.

military-superiority.rationale: Nationalists wanted an Egyptian army under national control but never stated a doctrine of superiority over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Egyptian nationalism is described as typically civic, stressing unity across ethnicity and religion.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Egyptian nationalism, as described, stresses unity across ethnicity and religion, the national struggle against occupation, and rejects class conflict as the driver.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Wafd was centre-right liberal-conservative; no stated commitment to equal outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The concept of indigenous authority over traditional lands has no application in Egypt's national movement.

colonial-reparations.rationale: The movement complained of requisitions and the conscription of 1.5 million Egyptians but no reparations claim is documented.

civilizational-union.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid opposed pan-Islamic, pan-Arab and pan-Ottoman unions and held Egypt a distinct nation.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The nationalist sources do not take a stance on the morality of self-interest; their ethos was national duty and patriotic love of homeland, not egoism.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Kamil stressed love of homeland and order; the 1923 constitution has both rights and duties.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental philosophy is outside the movement's concerns.

limit-population.rationale: Population limitation was not debated in the nationalist sources, so no stance is documented.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Nationalists wanted Egyptian industrialisation, such as Bank Misr's mills and airlines.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Industrial development was sought, but not disruption of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Human enhancement is a modern debate that the movement never considered.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Algorithmic government is anachronistic for this movement.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption is a modern technology that the movement never faced.

restore-past-order.rationale: Pharaonism looked back to ancient Egypt for identity, but the movement pursued constitutional modernity and rejected restoring old rule.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid's utility argument favours pragmatism, but this was not a stated doctrine of the whole movement.

direct-action.rationale: The 1919 revolution involved mass demonstrations and strikes, but the movement worked chiefly through the Wafd delegation, parliament and negotiation.

means-match-ends.rationale: The movement used both strikes and negotiation; the sources show no principle that methods must mirror ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to the movement's modernising programme; inferred.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not a position of the movement.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Alien to the movement's liberal capitalist economics; inferred.

production-for-use.rationale: Banque Misr's enterprises were profit-making national firms; inferred.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The movement's national capitalists relied on profit, and the thesis is Marxist.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The movement united all classes and creeds under a parliamentary programme.

collective-farming.rationale: The constitution makes property inviolable; collectivisation is not a nationalist aim.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The Marxist thesis of capitalism's inevitable imperialism is not stated in the nationalist sources, although nationalists blamed Britain's imperial interests for occupation.

taxation-theft.rationale: The constitution establishes taxation by law with a parliamentary budget; anti-tax doctrine is alien.

harm-principle.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid introduced Mill to Arab readers, yet the constitution limits liberties by law and morals; split.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The constitution protects individual rights while the nationalist movement framed rights through the nation; the claim that groups have no rights is inferred as not accepted.

conscription.rationale: The constitution says law prescribes conscription and army system.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The movement fought for participation in an elected parliament, not exit.

state-as-business.rationale: The constitution presents the state as a sovereign body; the business model is alien.

positive-liberty.rationale: The constitution provides free compulsory primary education, but no wider doctrine of material conditions of freedom is stated.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The movement was a civic nationalism defined against racial theories of imperial rule, though Kamil voiced racist views about sub-Saharan Africans.

organic-representation.rationale: Article on parliament makes members represent the whole nation through elections, not corporate bodies.

total-state.rationale: The constitution lists protected freedoms of belief, press, association and education.

national-rebirth.rationale: Egyptian nationalists saw the 1919 revolution as a national awakening against stagnation and domination, and Mustafa Kamil called for national revival.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Kamil claimed Sudan by right of conquest, but that was recovery of a claimed Egyptian possession; general expansion is not a stated aim.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The nation, not oaths of personal loyalty, is the source of power in the constitution.

bound-labor.rationale: The constitution guarantees personal freedom; the peasant revolt in 1919 opposed the corvee and forced labour for the British.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Postmodern epistemology is absent from the movement's sources.

universal-morality.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid believed in universal rights and equality, but others stressed national distinction.

single-common-good.rationale: The sources record no theory of a single rationally derived common good, so the movement is treated as neutral.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed by the liberal-era movement; later Egyptian nationalism opposed Israel; inferred disagreement.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Egyptian nationalist sources do not discuss a diaspora right of return.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not applicable as Arabic is the language of Egypt, though Pharaonism did not revive Coptic.

school-vouchers.rationale: The constitution has public education regulated by law and free in public schools.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Constitutional budget rules but no stated fiscal doctrine.

economic-freedom.rationale: The movement supported property and enterprise but never argued that political freedom depends on economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: The movement demanded rule by constitutional law and publicly announced rules.

national-self-determination.rationale: The 1919 delegation sought independence at the Paris Peace Conference and the nationalists, relying on Wilson's Fourteen Points, demanded Egypt's right to govern itself.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid and Hussein were rationalist liberals, but the movement united with religious believers.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The constitution reserves rights and public posts to Egyptians; welfare for citizens only is inferred.

work-for-welfare.rationale: No welfare system with work conditions was part of the nationalist programme, so no view is recorded.

class-collaboration.rationale: The 1919 revolution united merchants, officials, peasants, workers and clerics under the national cause, and the Wafd offered conciliation boards.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Pharaonism and the Tutankhamun controversy made the preservation of national heritage central to the movement.

dominated-front.rationale: Kamil framed Egypt as an Eastern country sharing a fate with India and the Dutch East Indies, but the liberal-era territorial strand did not seek formal fronts.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers took part in the 1919 revolution under the national banner; inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Girls and boys got compulsory primary education, yet voting excluded women; split.

ban-interest.rationale: Banque Misr was a conventional bank, and the movement was not Islamist; the Brotherhood opposed it on religious grounds.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Article 3 forbids discrimination by origin, language or religion.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Not stated; Marxist concept, though nationalists did portray the occupation as serving Britain.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Fossil fuel policy is not discussed in the liberal-era sources, although Banque Misr did found mining and oil companies.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The constitution lets Egyptian nationality be set by law; no assimilation doctrine is stated.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy of this kind is not part of the movement; inferred from its civic character.

proportional-representation.rationale: The 1923 constitution used elections for the House but the sources do not say how seats should be allocated.

national-mission.rationale: Not addressed, though Young Egypt envisioned an Arab world led by Egypt.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Feminist structural analysis is not a position of these nationalist sources.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Wafd criticised the Palace and British-supported governments, but not elites generally; split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not a position of the movement.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for past security force abuses is not covered in the sources on this movement, though nationalists protested British repression in 1919.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The constitution provides state education and public services; a minimal state is not proposed.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Equality clause and civic nationalism rule it out.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Article 3 sets equality before the law in rights and duties, though not universal as to women.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The movement fought British colonial occupation; inferred for settler states.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Freedom of belief was protected and family status was left to religious communities; low confidence.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Freedom of belief is absolute under Article 12.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not a position in Egypt; inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The constitution safeguards religious rites and Islam is the state religion; religious instruction in schools was customary.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The constitution declares that the source of all powers is the nation.

trade-surplus.rationale: Harb wanted Egyptian-owned industry but the sources do not state an export surplus goal.

population-transfer.rationale: Article 7 bars expelling Egyptians from the territory except by law, and the movement stressed unity.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Strikes and some violence against occupation were accepted; absolute principle not held.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Not addressed; the Wafd itself was later banned.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The movement framed British rule as arbitrary domination over Egypt; the general republican idea is inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: The 1923 constitution divides power among King, ministers, parliament and courts.

vanguard-party.rationale: The 1919 revolution was a mass national movement rather than led by a disciplined vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Wafd was landowner-led; no stated priority.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Public housing and tenant purchase rights have no counterpart in the nationalist sources.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Wafd could not change government anti-union policy; strikes were used in 1919.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian explanations of poverty were not a feature of the nationalist programme, which blamed foreign control.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The movement presented Muslim-Christian diversity as national strength, symbolised by crescent and cross.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Constitutional offices are filled by election or appointment.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The constitution lets the King declare martial law subject to parliament's review, so adherents accept limited emergency powers while demanding legal limits.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls on foods are not discussed in the sources, so no position is recorded.

party-controls-media.rationale: The constitution prohibits press censorship and guarantees free opinion.

party-commands-army.rationale: Army powers lie with law, King and parliament in the 1923 constitution.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Nationality is set by law; no stated period.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay of representatives is not discussed in the 1923 constitution summary nor other sources used here.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The Wafd ran as a disciplined mass party under Zaghloul but there was no binding doctrine.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Nationalists fought for sovereignty and rejected pan-Arab and pan-Islamic projects in the territorial strand.

head-commands-forces.rationale: In the 1923 constitution the King is supreme commander but acts through ministers.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not relevant to Egyptian nationalism, which is not centred on a hierarchical church.

clerical-rule.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid rejected religion as a basis of nationhood and authority; the 1923 constitution vests power in the nation.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not part of the movement; Marxist idea.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The constitution guards free opinion within law and public morals; limited morals censorship was accepted in practice.

recall-officials.rationale: Members represent the whole nation and voters may not instruct them.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The movement wanted British troops out but not an end to all alliances.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Alien to the movement and property-respecting.

people-in-arms.rationale: The constitution provides a regular army with conscription.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The sources record no doctrine on rural versus urban moral life, although the peasantry took part in the 1919 revolt.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The nationalists sought the unity of Egypt and Sudan, which Britain separated as a condominium.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The movement was led by educated professionals such as Lutfi al-Sayyid and Hussein.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Pharaonism praised ancient Egypt's greatness but also wanted Egypt to join the civilised nations; mixed.

death-penalty.rationale: The constitution forbids confiscation but does not ban capital punishment; Egyptian law retained it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The sources describe girls' compulsory primary schooling but nothing on sex education, and conservative norms make it unlikely to have been favoured.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The curriculum debate over evolution is not documented in the nationalist sources used here.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Public morals limits in the constitution; inferred.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Nationality is determined by law; descent versus territory not stated.

minority-language-support.rationale: Article 16 leaves use of any language unrestricted in private and religious life, but Arabic is the sole official language.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Article 13 safeguards religious rites subject to public order.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Lutfi al-Sayyid read Mill but the movement did not state this.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Constitution protects debt obligations in the budget; no cancellation demand.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Harb's Banque Misr aimed at economic independence alongside political independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The nationalists demanded a constitution written by Egyptian representatives rather than granted by the palace or Britain, though the 1923 text was drafted by a commission and promulgated by the King.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Wafd sought a free parliament and lost faith when it was sidelined.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear deterrence is anachronistic for a movement ending around 1952.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Head of state was a hereditary king.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Harb wanted a national bank, but the sources do not discuss central bank independence from government.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The sources record claims to Sudan but no stance on trading land for peace.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The constitution makes property inviolable but allows expropriation for public benefit with fair compensation.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The debate over the Soviet system's nature was not a nationalist concern, and the sources are silent.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk regulation is anachronistic for this movement.

collective-defense.rationale: Egypt's treaty position with Britain is documented, but nothing states a view on collective defence pacts among allies.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The nationalists considered the British protectorate imposed without consent as unlawful; inferred.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Constitution budget includes the Ministry of Religious Endowments; state oversight of clergy was common but not stated.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The constitution makes the king inviolable and ministers responsible, so the monarch stands above party in principle, though the Wafd clashed with the Palace.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The movement insisted on keeping Egypt and Sudan together, inferred from Kamil's and the Wafd's Sudan claims.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The nationalists wanted a unified state, and no source discusses autonomous regions with separate systems.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The constitution makes the king a constitutional monarch under the nation's laws, not divine.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax rate structures are not discussed in the sources on the Wafd or Banque Misr.

character-from-environment.rationale: The sources do not discuss theories of character formation, so it is left neutral.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The 1923 constitution binds the King to swear to respect the constitution and laws of the Egyptian nation.

space-expansion.rationale: Space expansion is anachronistic for this movement.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The 1923 constitution mixes a hereditary King, an partly appointed Senate and an elected House.

leader-cult.rationale: Zaghloul was honoured as a national hero and the Wafd's Blue Shirts leaned toward leader loyalty, but it did not claim embodiment of the nation.

equal-parenting.rationale: Child custody presumptions are absent from the nationalist sources, and family law was left to religious communities.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: This is a debate within Marxist-Leninist thought, not part of the Egyptian nationalist sources.

land-redistribution.rationale: Constitution makes property inviolable and Wafd leaders were landowners; land reform came with the 1952 Free Officers.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return rights are not addressed in the nationalist sources used here.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Egyptian territorial nationalism rests on the Nile Valley rather than co-ethnic claims.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The 1923 constitution declares freedom of belief absolute (Article 12), which rules out punishing apostasy.

women-must-cover.rationale: Women took part in public demonstrations in 1919 and the movement did not require covering.

common-currency.rationale: Currency union was not part of the movement's programme, although Harb's national bank aimed at Egyptian financial independence.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Taha Hussein said the Egyptian is Pharaonic before being Arab, rejecting political unity of Arabic-speaking peoples.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The movement sought a single unified national community.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The movement held that Copts and Muslims should win rights together in Egypt rather than separate.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The 1923 constitution created a parliament with lawmaking power, and the Wafd's slogan placed the nation above the government, but the king retained a veto and decrees.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Wafd was a mass party organisation with formal structures.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Liberal-era nationalists never addressed pollution or resource taxes, and there is nothing to infer a side from.

future-generations.rationale: Not an ecological theme for the movement; its concern for the nation's lasting heritage and independence implies a duty to hand on Egypt to later generations, inferred.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Nationalists such as Qasim Amin's circle and the Wafd women's movement backed women's role in the nation, but there is no stated claim of distinct values; adherents are split.

arms-reduction.rationale: The movement sought the end of British occupation and an Egyptian army under the 1923 constitution; it left no doctrine on reducing armaments.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Nationalists demanded open treaty negotiation at times against the secret Anglo-Egyptian dealings, but left no general doctrine, so it is treated as unsettled.

capital-controls.rationale: Talaat Harb's economic nationalism sought Egyptian-owned banks and firms against foreign capital, so limiting capital movement is inferred, though no controls were demanded.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: A constitutional state under Wafd-era liberal nationalism implies a state monopoly on force; inferred from the 1923 constitution's order of state authority.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The movement fought for national independence and an army under the nation's own constitution, so refusal of orders is unlikely; inferred.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Liberal-era nationalists such as Talaat Harb built Egyptian capital but left no stated doctrine on bargaining; the Wafd later backed labour organisation, so adherents are split.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The tax-credit mechanism is anachronistic and the movement left no record; no inference possible.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: The 1923 constitution set up parliamentary control of the budget but no borrowing limits; Egyptian debt to Europe was a grievance, so adherents are split.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The movement stressed Egyptian ownership of the economy against foreign domination, so changing rules in favour of poorer states is inferred.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Liberal nationalists sought a constitutional order through parliament and treaty negotiation rather than smashing the state; inferred from the Wafd's constitutional strategy.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: No blueprint was set by the movement, but Egyptian economic nationalism favoured national development within a market economy; adherents split.

nature-as-capital.rationale: The movement predates ecological accounting and left no position.

sacred-nation.rationale: Egyptian nationalism treats the nation as a historic, enduring community of Muslims and Copts rooted in the Nile Valley, though it is mostly civic rather than sacral.

student-debt-relief.rationale: The movement predates student loans and has no stated position.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The movement was anti-colonial but centred on the Egyptian-British relationship and left no stated view on regional exploitation inside Egypt.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Liberal-era nationalists such as Lutfi al-Sayyid drew on natural-rights liberalism, implying a shared human nature behind rights; inferred.

public-service-media.rationale: The movement left no doctrine on public broadcasting, which only emerged later.

religions-one-truth.rationale: The movement united Muslims and Copts as one nation without taking a theological position on whether religions share one truth.

farm-price-support.rationale: Economic nationalists such as Talaat Harb backed Egyptian-owned finance; protection of farmers from moneylenders is inferred from that programme.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the emphasis on national independence and strength.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Wafd was a cross-class national front, so a separate workers' party is inferred to be outside its programme.

ban-fgm.rationale: Modernist liberals such as Lutfi al-Sayyid favoured social reform; a legal ban is inferred, not documented.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance remained under Islamic law and the liberal nationalists did not challenge it; adherents are not documented as taking a side.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Arabic is the national language in the 1923 constitution; inferred that the nation is seen as having one language.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from a state-led developmentalist outlook rather than private-law remedies.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The programme was a constitution and elected parliament, with no role for customary chiefs.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: The movement never addressed environmental questions; liberal-era nationalists valued individual liberty but no position is documented.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; liberal constitutionalists favoured judicial independence but no sentencing position is documented.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Arabic is the official language under the 1923 constitution; a language requirement is inferred.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The Wafd-era movement left no doctrine on union membership rules; adherents are split, inferred from its silence on labor law.

voter-id.rationale: The 1923 constitution set electoral rules by law but the nationalists took no stated line on voter identification; adherents are split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Muslim-Christian unity under the slogan "Religion is for God, the homeland for all" is inferred to favour equal standing of interpretations, though the 1923 constitution made Islam the state religion.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Nationalists demanded an elected parliament and constitution, inferred to mean legitimacy rests on elections, though they also cared about national independence.

premarital-sex.rationale: Liberal-era nationalists were socially conservative on sexuality, inferred from the period and the absence of any stated reform position.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the liberal constitutional commitment to freedom of expression and the press in the 1923 constitution.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Anachronistic; the nationalists favoured Egyptian ownership of the economy and no such cash-transfer doctrine, so rejection is inferred.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women joined the 1919 revolution but the 1923 constitution gave votes to men only and the Wafd did not push suffrage; a mildly supportive view is inferred from the liberal outlook.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Inferred from the movement's secular-liberal but respectful stance toward Islam and Coptic Christianity; it did not blame religion for women's position.

race-social-construct.rationale: Pharaonist identity stressed cultural continuity rather than race theory, and no stated view on racial categories exists; adherents are split.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Dedicated state agencies for gender equality were unknown in the period and the movement took no position.

notes: Most sources are Wikipedia articles plus the 1923 constitution as the one primary text; economic and social answers are largely inferred. Nasser-era pan-Arab nationalism would answer civilizational and kin-union statements differently. Mustafa Kamil's Ottoman loyalty and Sudan claims differ from Lutfi al-Sayyid's territorial strand.
